analysis.one_liner: Exempts most over-the-counter derivatives deals between large institutions from federal regulation.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 377-4 on October 19, 2000, with only four members opposed, and the measure became law that December after the Senate attached a revised version to a year-end spending bill.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites federal derivatives law. It declares that most over-the-counter derivatives — privately negotiated contracts between banks and other big institutions on interest rates, currencies, and other financial measures — are outside the Commodity Exchange Act, so the Commodity Futures Trading Commission does not regulate them. It also sets shared SEC–CFTC rules for futures on individual stocks, lets banks operate clearing organizations for these contracts, preempts some state law, and reauthorizes the CFTC's funding through 2005. Alongside that, it gives the CFTC new power to police retail foreign-currency scams sold to ordinary people.
analysis.who_benefits: Large banks and swaps dealers gain legally certain, enforceable contracts without Commodity Futures Trading Commission review, registration, or oversight of their products. Futures exchanges and electronic trading platforms gain authority to trade new products, including futures on individual stocks. Agricultural producers get procedures to make hedging easier, and retail customers of foreign-exchange firms gain a federal regulator policing fraud in that market.

how_it_helps.text: Excludes over-the-counter derivatives in interest rates, currencies, and other financial measures traded between 'eligible contract participants' from the Commodity Exchange Act, giving those contracts 'legal certainty' — enforceability without Commission review of the products [S3][S4].
Excludes individually negotiated swap agreements between big institutions from the Commodity Exchange Act entirely [S3][S4].
Lets banks and their affiliates operate multilateral clearing organizations that net out over-the-counter derivative exposures, which the bill describes as reducing systemic risk [S3][S4].
Creates a joint SEC and Commodity Futures Trading Commission framework so futures on individual stocks can legally trade in the United States, with the SEC overseeing the trading [S3].

Gives the Commodity Futures Trading Commission explicit authority over retail foreign-currency contracts sold to people who are not institutional traders, aimed at 'bucket shops' that might otherwise go unregulated [S4].
Reauthorizes CFTC appropriations through fiscal year 2005, requires the agency to weigh costs and benefits before most rules, and directs it to consider rules encouraging producer hedging [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the cost in the form of a fast-growing derivatives market operating with little federal oversight: no regulator tracks the exposures building up among big dealers, and the fraud and manipulation rules that govern exchange-traded futures largely do not reach these contracts. Ordinary investors are effectively locked out of the deregulated market, since only institutions and wealthy individuals qualify to trade in it, and state consumer law is preempted for security-futures transactions. If a major dealer fails, losses can spread through banks to the broader economy.
analysis.who_pays_short: Anyone exposed when derivatives markets fail

drawbacks.text: Only institutions meeting asset thresholds and individuals with more than $10 million (or $5 million for hedging their own risk) in assets count as 'eligible contract participants,' so the deregulated derivatives market is reserved for large institutions and the wealthy, outside the protections of regulated exchanges [S4].

The bill removes most CFTC oversight — including its anti-fraud and market-policing authority — from the over-the-counter swaps market, the fastest-growing part of the derivatives business, leaving those contracts largely outside federal review [S3][S4].
It preempts state law over security-futures transactions, leaving only state antifraud laws of general application [S3].

It requires the Commission to consider costs and benefits before issuing most rules and states that excluded transactions cannot be presumed covered, making it harder for the regulator to reach new derivative products as they emerge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Legal certainty for swaps and authorized clearing of derivatives had real value to banks and arguably to the stability of contract enforcement, and the retail foreign-exchange provisions add a genuine consumer protection. But the bill's central choice — keeping the multi-trillion-dollar over-the-counter derivatives market outside federal oversight — removed the main tool for seeing and limiting risk-building across the financial system. Eight years later, lightly regulated credit-default swaps written by a few large dealers were central to the 2008 financial crisis, which cost ordinary people jobs, homes, and savings. The consumer protections in the bill are real but small next to what was taken off the regulator's desk.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 377-4 on October 19, 2000; the Senate never voted on it as a standalone bill, but that December it attached a revised version of this measure to a year-end appropriations bill, and President Clinton signed it into law as Public Law 106-554 on December 21, 2000.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Ewing introduced the bill on May 25, 2000, with three Republican cosponsors [S1][S5].
Three House committees — Agriculture, Banking and Financial Services, and Commerce — each held hearings, amended, and reported the bill during summer 2000 [S6].
The House passed it 377-4 on October 19, 2000 under 'suspension of the rules,' a fast-track procedure that requires a two-thirds majority and limits debate [S7][S6].
Both parties backed it overwhelmingly: 181 of 209 voting Democrats, 194 of 221 voting Republicans, and both independents voted yes; only four members voted no [S7].
The Senate received the bill on October 19, 2000 and never voted on it as a standalone measure before that Congress ended [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large banks and over-the-counter derivatives dealers came out ahead: their swaps contracts became legally certain and enforceable without Commodity Futures Trading Commission oversight, and futures exchanges gained authority to trade new products. That deregulated market later played a central role in the 2008 financial crisis, whose costs fell on ordinary people.

against.what_they_did: Warned beginning in 1998 that unregulated over-the-counter derivatives posed a systemic threat and sought CFTC authority over swaps; Congress and the other financial regulators blocked that effort, she resigned before this bill passed, and the bill wrote her agency out of that market.

sides.party_line_note: The vote was near-unanimous across parties — 181 of 209 voting Democrats, 194 of 221 voting Republicans, and both independents in favor, with only four no votes [S7].

industries.industry: Big banks and over-the-counter derivatives dealers
industries.note: The bill takes the privately negotiated swaps market — dominated by a handful of large dealers — out from under Commodity Futures Trading Commission oversight and lets banks operate clearing organizations for these contracts. The industry's interest in minimal oversight runs against the public's interest in transparent, supervised markets where systemic risk can be seen and limited.

industries.industry: Futures exchanges and electronic trading platforms
industries.note: Exchanges gain authority to operate electronic trading facilities, trade new products, and list futures on individual stocks, with much of their oversight shifted to self-regulation under broad 'core principles.' Some of that latitude comes at the expense of the market policing the CFTC previously exercised.

Deals in 'exempt commodities' — anything that is not an agricultural commodity or a financial measure, which includes energy products — made electronically between large commercial entities are excluded from the Act. Traders gain freedom from oversight; the public loses a check on manipulation in markets that feed into energy and commodity prices.

The bill creates a new single-stock futures market that broker-dealers and futures merchants can intermediate under expedited registration, with exemptions from some investor-protection requirements such as SIPC membership. It opens new business lines while lightening the rules attached to them.

The bill gives the CFTC explicit jurisdiction over retail foreign-currency contracts sold to non-institutional customers, closing a gap that fraud schemes had exploited. This is a consumer protection that runs against the operators of those schemes.
